parts: A thermodynamic system is described by its state variables: pressure, volume and temperature.
Thermal equilibrium: two bodies in contact exchange no heat when they are at the same temperature.
Zeroth law: if A and B are each in thermal equilibrium with C, then A and B are in equilibrium with each other. This defines temperature, which decides the direction of heat flow.
A system is in thermodynamic equilibrium when it is in thermal, mechanical and chemical equilibrium at the same time.
Heat is energy in transit because of a temperature difference, measured in joules. 1 cal = 4.186 J and 1 kcal ≈ 4186 J (J is the mechanical equivalent of heat).

Internal energy U is the total kinetic and potential energy of the molecules. It is a function of state and does not depend on how the state was reached. For an ideal gas, U depends only on temperature. Heat is closely associated with the random kinetic energy of molecules.
Work done by a gas is W = ∫P dV, the area under the P–V (indicator) diagram. In an isobaric process W = P(V₂ − V₁).
ΔQ = ΔU + ΔW, where ΔQ is the heat supplied, ΔU the rise in internal energy and ΔW the work done by the system. Work done on the system increases U.
Examples: 110 J supplied with ΔU = 40 J gives W = 70 J. Absorbing 2000 J while doing 500 J of work gives ΔU = 1500 J. Absorbing 1100 J while 400 J of work is done on the system gives ΔU = 1500 J.
Limitations: the first law does not tell the direction of heat flow, the conditions under which heat can be converted to work, or how much of it can be.
Isothermal (T constant): the process is slow, in a conducting vessel. ΔU = 0, so Q = W, and PV = constant.
Adiabatic (Q = 0): the process is fast, in an insulated vessel. ΔU = −W, and PV^γ = constant. A gas cools when it expands adiabatically, because it does work using its own internal energy.
Isobaric (P constant): the indicator diagram is a horizontal line. Isochoric (V constant): W = 0.

A reversible process can be retraced exactly through the same states, as in very slow frictionless compression. Irreversible processes include friction, free expansion and heat flowing across a temperature difference. All natural processes are irreversible.
Kelvin–Planck statement: no engine working in a cycle can convert all the heat it takes in into work, so 100% efficiency is impossible.
Clausius statement: heat cannot flow by itself from a colder body to a hotter one.
A heat engine takes Q₁ from a source at T₁, does work W and rejects Q₂ to a sink at T₂. Its efficiency is η = W/Q₁ = 1 − Q₂/Q₁.

The Carnot engine is an ideal reversible engine. Its cycle is isothermal expansion, adiabatic expansion, isothermal compression and adiabatic compression. Its efficiency η = 1 − T₂/T₁ (kelvin) is independent of the working substance, and no real engine between T₁ and T₂ can be more efficient.
η = 100% would need T₂ = 0 K, which cannot be reached.
Examples: between the steam point and the ice point, η = 1 − 273/373 ≈ 26.8%. Between 227 °C and 27 °C, η = 40%. With the sink at 27 °C and η = 25%, the source is at 400 K.
A refrigerator is a heat engine run in reverse. Left open in a closed room it warms the room, because it rejects the heat it removes plus the work done by its motor.
